vignette:
Tui used to love the annual publishing gala—the clink of champagne glasses, the buzz of deal-making, the warm press of colleagues. That night five years ago, when faulty wiring set the ballroom’s drapery ablaze and the exits sealed into a crush, he became a survivor among those who did not. He remembers the smoke coiling into chandeliers, the screams, the man in front of him falling and not getting up. Those images are terrifyingly clear and mostly visual, like a film that plays behind his eyelids without warning. Waking from nightmares still saturated with that orange glow, he often finds the smell of alcohol clinging to his sheets—dream residue, he calls it, but it also clings to any real-world scent of beer or wine. Just last week a colleague’s breath at an editorial meeting made him physically recoil. 

He has come to believe that staying hypervigilant is the only way to stay safe. At home in suburban Seattle, Tui is alert even in his own living room: he always positions himself so his back is against a wall, a habit that has turned every chair into a potential risk until it is properly placed. When he goes out for coffee, he cannot help scanning the room—checking exits, watching hands, listening for raised voices. Ordinary sounds startle him; his wife’s footsteps on the stairs can make him jump, and he feels the flush of shame afterward. That persistent sense of imminent danger kept him anchored to the event in his mind, pulling memories forward no matter how hard he tried to leave them behind. That constant watchfulness feels necessary, yet it seems to bring the worst memories closer. When he is on guard, the flames flash into his mind more vividly, and the need to avoid everything connected to that evening grows stronger. He has stopped seeing friends entirely, especially those from the publishing circle who might mention the gala. Steering clear of friends who might speak of the gala meant that their faces, their voices, even their names became loaded with the memory—the avoidance itself had charged them with danger. 

In the months after the fire, Tui’s checking and scanning became automatic. He noticed that every time he made himself sit with his back exposed, a wave of panic followed, so he simply never did. By never exposing his back, he had sealed off the chance to learn that the threat might not be as constant as he imagined—his body had only received confirmation that the precautions were necessary, keeping the sense of danger locked at its peak. Over time, the isolation hardened. His wife worries he has become a stranger; he knows he has. Now, when a news report or a conversation forces him to talk about the disaster, the memories surge uncontrollably—and he also finds himself scanning the room mid-sentence, which only makes the images stronger. He has come to his first appointment because his daughter’s wedding is approaching and the hotel ballroom terrifies him, and he is desperate not to ruin that day. But he is equally afraid that if he lets his guard down even for a moment, something terrible will happen again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes intrusive memories; it shows that hypervigilance (a maladaptive strategy) brings memories, but not the threat itself.
There is no causal relationship where maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) lead to the creation or intensification of triggers; triggers are linked to memories instead.
The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies cause an increased sense of threat; rather, threat is the reason for adopting the strategies.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that the sense of threat directly causes intrusive memories; it shows that hypervigilance (a maladaptive strategy) brings memories, but not the threat itself.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: There is no causal relationship where maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) lead to the creation or intensification of triggers; triggers are linked to memories instead.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies cause an increased sense of threat; rather, threat is the reason for adopting the strategies.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
